title: Four Defaults Schools Should Question
author: Eric Hudson
summary: Eric Hudson applies Joy Buolamwini's concept of 'default settings' — which reflect the priorities and prejudices of technology designers — to schooling itself. He identifies four school defaults that AI reveals as choices rather than immutable facts: devices-first classrooms (should become devices-as-needed), teacher-decided technology policies (should become teaching students how to decide), student-only use policies (should become community-wide use policies), and AI-as-EdTech (should become AI-as-infrastructure). The core insight is that defaults are easy to accept and hard to change because they exploit the cognitive anchoring bias. Schools that examine these defaults can move toward more intentional, agentic approaches to technology — for both teachers and students.
points: Default settings in technology reflect designer priorities and prejudices — they are choices, not neutral starting points, and the same is true of school defaults.
Devices-first classrooms make AI-assisted bypassing of thinking effortless; the default should shift to devices-as-needed based on learning purpose.
Teaching students how to decide when and why to use technology is more valuable than adults making those decisions for them.
AI use policies framed only around student behavior miss the broader ecosystem where teachers and administrators also use AI in schools.
Treating AI as just another EdTech tool misses that AI is becoming infrastructure — as foundational as electricity or the internet to how knowledge and learning function.
quotes: Default settings 'often reflect the coded gaze… the machines we build reflect the priorities, preferences, and even prejudices of those who have the power to shape technology.'
Recognizing defaults as choices made for us by someone else is the first step towards changing our relationship with defaults.
Beginning a class with a conversation or with some quiet writing in journals or with group work at the board are all device-free, AI-resistant learning strategies.
We should not treat the decision to allow or restrict technology as equivalent to teaching students how to use it.
Treating AI as just another tool to add to our classroom toolkit misses how fundamentally AI is changing the nature of knowledge, learning, and even what it means to be educated.
